titles.Neighbouring organs: Bladder, urethra, ureters, rectum and anus

clinical: Pelvic shape in childbirth
The size and shape of the bony pelvic inlet and outlet set the passage a baby must pass through during labour.
Slipped disc at L5/S1
A herniated lumbosacral (L5/S1) disc, with L4/5 the other common site, can press on a spinal nerve root and cause back pain radiating down the leg (sciatica).
Pelvic organ prolapse
Weakened levator ani and supporting tissue, often after vaginal childbirth, can let the bladder, uterus or rectum sag down into the vagina. This is called prolapse.
Stress incontinence
Pelvic floor weakness is a common cause of stress urinary incontinence, where urine leaks on coughing, sneezing or lifting.
Fibroids
Uterine fibroids (leiomyomas) are benign smooth muscle tumours of the myometrium, common in women of reproductive age. They can cause heavy periods and pelvic pressure.
Postpartum haemorrhage
After delivery the myometrium must contract to compress the vessels of the placental site. Failure to contract (uterine atony) is the commonest cause of severe bleeding after childbirth.
Cervical screening
Most cervical cancers arise in the transformation zone, where squamous and columnar epithelium meet. This is the area sampled at cervical screening.
HPV infection
Almost all cervical cancers are caused by persistent infection with high-risk types of human papillomavirus (HPV).
Vaginal atrophy after menopause
Falling oestrogen after the menopause thins the squamous lining of the vagina, causing dryness, soreness and painful intercourse.
Ectopic pregnancy
Most ectopic pregnancies implant in the uterine tube, usually in the ampulla, and can rupture causing severe internal bleeding.
Salpingitis
Infection of the tube can scar and block it, causing infertility and raising the risk of ectopic pregnancy.
Polycystic ovary syndrome
A common hormonal disorder that causes irregular ovulation and raised androgen levels. The ovaries often show many small peripheral follicles on ultrasound.
Ovarian torsion
The ovary can twist on its blood-vessel pedicle, cutting off its blood supply and causing sudden severe pelvic pain that needs urgent surgery.
Uterine prolapse
The cardinal and uterosacral ligaments help hold the cervix and uterus in place. Stretching of these supports, together with pelvic floor weakness, contributes to uterine prolapse.
Round ligament pain
Sharp pain in the groin during the second trimester is often round ligament pain, caused by stretching as the uterus enlarges.
Endometriosis

Endometriosis is growth of endometrial-type tissue outside the uterus. It commonly implants on the pelvic peritoneum, including the rectouterine pouch, and on the ovaries, causing pelvic pain and sometimes infertility.
Fluid in the rectouterine pouch
Blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy, or pus, can collect in the rectouterine pouch and can be felt on vaginal examination of the posterior fornix.
Bleeding after childbirth
Severe postpartum bleeding can be controlled by embolising the uterine arteries, which is less invasive than tying the internal iliac arteries.
Ureter injury in hysterectomy
The ureter runs beneath the uterine artery close to the cervix, so it is at risk of injury during hysterectomy.
Urinary tract infection
The short female urethra lies close to the vagina and anus, making urinary tract infection, especially cystitis (bladder infection), much more common in women than men.
Bladder injury at caesarean section
The bladder sits in front of the lower uterine segment and can be injured during caesarean section, especially where there are adhesions.
Bartholin's cyst
Blocked Bartholin's (greater vestibular) glands can form a painful cyst or abscess beside the vaginal opening.
Perineal tears
Tears of the vestibule and perineal body are common in vaginal childbirth, and both tears and episiotomies are repaired in layers.
Breast cancer
Most breast cancers arise from the ducts or lobules. A tumour that pulls on the suspensory (Cooper's) ligaments can dimple the overlying skin.
Mastitis
A blocked lactiferous duct in a breastfeeding woman can become infected, causing a red, painful breast (mastitis).
Ovarian cancer
Ovarian epithelial tumours, the most common ovarian cancers, were long thought to arise from this surface layer. They are often diagnosed late because early symptoms are vague.
Hilus cell tumour
Rare hilus cell tumours of the ovary can produce androgens, causing virilisation such as facial hair and a deeper voice.
Scarring from salpingitis
Infection of the tube can scar and fuse the mucosal folds, blocking the lumen and trapping the embryo, which can cause ectopic pregnancy.
Asherman's syndrome
Scarring of the endometrium, often after curettage or uterine surgery, causes thin or absent periods and can lead to infertility.
Endometrial cancer
Endometrial cancer typically presents with abnormal or postmenopausal bleeding, so any such bleeding needs investigation.
Fertile window
Conception is only possible in the few days before ovulation and about a day after it. The egg survives about 24 hours, while sperm can survive several days in the female tract.
IVF
In IVF the egg is fertilised in a laboratory dish and the embryo is transferred to the uterus, often at the blastocyst stage.
